KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Coffee Maker — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the coffee maker as the kitchen’s most familiar hands-off machine: it hums, it drips, and the child’s job is to let it work — while owning the cold drinks.

What is this?

A coffee maker drips hot water through coffee grounds into a glass jug, and its plate keeps the jug hot all morning. Hot machine, hot jug — a look-and-learn member of the hot family.

What does it mean?

The coffee maker is a low-drama place to rehearse the hot rule: nothing about it invites touch. Children learn that some machines are watched, named and left alone — a whole category of safety in one appliance.

What does the child need to know?

You need the machine and the brew ritual, watched from outside: water in, filter in, button on — "drip, drip, drip." The rule: "the jug is hot; grown-ups pour." The counter-offer: your child pours the COLD drinks.

Why this matters

A child with a real pouring job (juice! water!) stays in the serving business safely, while the hot rule lands where it belongs — on the machine that is genuinely hot.

What it teaches

Machine-watching patience, the hot-rule rehearsal, pouring control (cold side), and the family-roles picture: who runs which machine.

Words to learn

coffee makerdripfilterjughotpour

Say this to your child

“"Coffee maker! Drip, drip, drip — the morning machine. Water in, coffee in… the jug fills up. The jug is HOT — grown-ups only. And YOUR job: the cold drinks! Juice for everyone — pour with two hands!"”

Step by step

  1. Name the machine: "coffee maker! The morning machine."
  2. Watch a brew from the outside: "water in the top… coffee in the filter… button — drip, drip, drip!"
  3. The rule while it drips: "the jug gets HOT. The coffee maker is a grown-up machine — we watch."
  4. The counter-offer at the fridge: "YOUR pouring job — the cold drinks! Juice for the table… water for the cups."
  5. Pour and serve. Two pouring jobs, two temperatures, one safe system.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "coffee maker" sit over a drip machine with its glass jug — the jug about to fill, drop by patient drop.

Ask your child

"What does the coffee maker do?" (drips) "Who pours the coffee?" (grown-ups — the jug is hot) "What is YOUR pouring job?" (the cold drinks)

What your child can say or do

Your child might narrate every drip, referee the jug from afar ("HOT!"), or pour juice for the whole table — both jobs, both temperatures.

Out in the real world

Coffee machines hum in every kitchen and hotel. Each brew is a free rehearsal: "dripping… the jug is hot… my job is the juice." Roles confirmed, everywhere.

Try it together

Family Café: the cold-drink station is the child’s — jug of juice, cups, two-hand pouring, orders taken. The coffee maker hums in the background, officially out of bounds and therefore uninteresting.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the coffee maker make?" (coffee) "Is the jug hot?" (yes — all morning) "What do YOU pour?" (cold drinks!)

Staying safe

The jug and the plate under it stay hot for hours — long after the drip stops. Rule: the coffee maker is a grown-up machine, watched and named; the child owns the cold-drink pouring.

This lesson pairs with the Coffee Maker flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.
